opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about the gap. If you add up all the images and video on the internet, it sounds enormous, but it doesn't look much like what a person actually sees growing up. A child takes in a continuous, first-person, embodied stream: they move their head, reach for things, walk around objects, and see what happens when they push something off a table. Internet data is mostly curated snapshots, framed and edited by photographers for other humans. So it's not just a question of scale. The distribution is different.

So how do you begin? A few directions seem promising to me.

One is egocentric data. There have already been efforts with head-mounted cameras, including datasets recorded from infants' perspectives and large first-person video collections. They're still small compared to a lifetime of vision, but they show that this kind of data is learnable and carries signals you don't get from web images, like temporal continuity, motion, and cause and effect.

Second, wearable devices are going to change the picture. As smart glasses and similar hardware become more common, the infrastructure for capturing continuous visual experience will exist almost by default. That raises serious privacy and consent questions, and I think the research community has to take those seriously from day one rather than treating them as an afterthought. But technically, that's probably where scale will come from.

Third is simulation and world models. You can't simulate everything faithfully, but you can generate interactive experience where the agent's actions change what it sees next. That closed loop of acting and observing is something passive datasets fundamentally lack.

And finally, I'd say we should also rethink what "data" means for vision. Maybe the goal isn't to match the raw number of pixels a human sees, but to capture the right structure: persistence, three-dimensional space, interaction. Humans are remarkably data-efficient partly because the data they get is so structured. If we only chase volume, we may end up with more of the wrong thing.

So I'd start small but in the right form, with embodied, continuous, interactive data, learn what matters from it, and then scale.

r001.rationale: The response recommends egocentric recordings, wearable cameras, and simulation as promising directions. It does not propose existing YouTube videos as the initial data source.

r002.rationale: The response gives no comparison between YouTube uploads in thirty minutes and four months of a child's visual experience.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because when you look at how a child learns to see, the numbers are humbling. By the time a kid is three or four years old, they've taken in something on the order of hundreds of millions of visual frames, continuously, embodied, from a first-person view, with their own actions driving what they see next. No dataset we have today looks anything like that. ImageNet is a few million curated photos. Even the big web-scale image-text sets are, at the end of the day, a collection of snapshots that other people decided were worth posting. It's a very biased slice of the world.

So the honest answer is that I don't think we get there by scraping harder. I think there are a few directions that have to come together.

The first is egocentric video. Projects like Ego4D, or the earlier SAYCam work where researchers literally put head-mounted cameras on infants, are tiny by internet standards, but they're the right kind of data. It's continuous, it has temporal structure, it has the camera moving through space the way a body moves. I'd love to see that scaled by orders of magnitude, and I think wearable devices are going to make that possible almost as a side effect, as long as we can solve the privacy and consent problems, which are real and not something to hand-wave past.

The second is video more broadly. Even passive internet video is far closer to human visual experience than static images, because the world reveals its 3D structure through motion. Objects persist, occlusions resolve, physics plays out. A lot of what a self-supervised model needs to learn about the visual world is already there in the temporal dimension, and we've barely scratched it.

The third is simulation and synthetic data. People are a bit allergic to this because of the sim-to-real gap, but if you want billions of frames with action labels, depth, and consistent geometry, rendering is the cheapest way to get them. The trick is using it to learn the structural priors, the things that are true in any world, and letting real data handle the texture of this one.

And then the last thing, which is maybe more of a philosophical point, is that I'm not sure matching the human scale of raw pixels is actually the goal. A child doesn't just see; a child acts, gets feedback, asks questions, gets corrected by a parent. The data is interactive. So when we talk about "human-scale visual experience," I'd push us to think about it as collecting experience rather than collecting frames. That probably means robots, or agents in environments, generating their own data loop. That's harder, but I think it's where the field is eventually going.

r001.rationale: The response recommends egocentric video and passive internet video broadly, but does not propose YouTube as the initial data source.

r002.rationale: It estimates a child's visual experience in frames by age three or four, but gives no comparison to the amount uploaded to YouTube in thirty minutes.

astra-6.text:
I think one starting point is to collect video from a first-person perspective. A lot of our datasets are collections of individual images, but that’s quite different from how humans experience the world. We see a continuous stream, and we move around, interact with objects, and observe what changes as a result of our actions.

So you could imagine people wearing cameras while going about their daily lives. That gives us a way to begin collecting visual experience at a much larger scale. Of course, privacy and consent would have to be part of the design from the beginning.

But I think the interesting question is not just how many hours we can collect. It’s what a model can learn from those hours. Adjacent frames can be very redundant, but over time you see an object from different viewpoints, you see people manipulating it, and you see cause and effect. Can a model use that structure without someone labeling every frame? To me, that’s the important connection between collecting data at this scale and learning from it.

r001.rationale: It proposes collecting first-person video, potentially with people wearing cameras, but does not identify existing YouTube videos as the initial data source.

r002.rationale: It gives no comparison between YouTube upload volume in thirty minutes and four months of a child’s visual experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to ask what we mean by the scale of human visual experience. It’s not just the number of images you’ve seen. You’re seeing a continuous world, you’re moving around, and your actions influence what you see next. There’s a lot of structure in that experience that a collection of independent images doesn’t capture.

One place to begin is video, especially video from a first-person perspective. That gives us continuity: the same object from different viewpoints, how things change over time, and how people interact with their surroundings. But collecting more hours is only part of the problem. We also need to understand the diversity of those experiences and what a model can actually learn from them.

So I would start with a manageable setting where we can connect visual observations with actions and outcomes, and then expand. The question isn’t only, ‘Can we collect as much data as a person sees?’ It’s also, ‘Are we collecting the kinds of experience that make that data useful?’

r001.rationale: The response suggests first-person video as a starting point, but does not propose using existing YouTube videos.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention YouTube uploads in thirty minutes or compare that volume to four months of a child’s visual experience.
